hook: Nick Cammarata is an interpretability researcher at Goodfire and the author of Neural Networks Are Already Clean (15 October 2026), an essay arguing that the neurons of neural networks can mostly be read directly and that superposition, the explanation he helped name, misread the evidence. Earlier, by the account on his own site, he did research at OpenAI on what neural networks learn and helped share that work through Distill, including the 2020 article Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits, written with Chris Olah.

quick_facts: Researcher at Goodfire, an AI interpretability research lab, and author of the essay Neural Networks Are Already Clean, published 15 October 2026 (essay byline).
Earlier role: his own site, nickcammarata.com, says he does research at OpenAI on what neural networks learn and is on the Distill team; the site is old and still names OpenAI as his employer.
Co-author, with Chris Olah and others, of Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits (Distill, 2020), which his site links as the work he helped share.

According to Implicator (16 October 2026), the essay contrasts an OpenAI project he started in 2023 to explain neurons, which could explain about 1.7 percent of the neurons studied, with his new audit of Qwen3-32B.
His site carries an older essay, The Abstraction Machine, arguing that neural network interpretability matters in its own right.

achievements.title: Neural Networks Are Already Clean, 2026
achievements.impact: An informal research essay and working hypothesis published by Goodfire. It argues that a polysemantic neuron usually shares a feature researchers missed, so that many neurons can be read directly without first being decomposed by a sparse autoencoder, and that monosemanticity is more common than thought: a preliminary audit of Qwen3-32B found about 90 percent of neuron poles with one main job. It has not been peer reviewed, and a technical companion paper has not yet been released.

achievements.title: Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits, 2020
achievements.impact: Co-authored the Distill article that introduced the circuits approach to reading neural networks neuron by neuron.
